Police and fire officials reported a large tree toppled by high winds as a severe thunderstorm moved across the region. The tree penetrated through portions of a home. The home was heavily damaged and was declared condemned.

A strong thunderstorm intensified to severe levels upon approach to the coast at Vero Beach. The storm produced winds which toppled a tree onto a house and caused damage to the roof. Nearby, the winds blew the arm of a construction crane into power lines, taking the lines down. Strong winds also blew a large tree limb down which took down power lines. The wind damage affected 16th street and the south side of Vero Beach south of the intersection of 4th Street and U.S. Highway 1. Damage reports were received from police officials and the Scripps Treasure Coast newspaper.
Strong thunderstorm winds gusted up to 43 knots at the Vero Beach Airport (KVRB) ASOS as the storm crossed into the adjacent coastal waters.
A thunderstorm passing offshore the peninsula produced another wind gust to 43 knots at the Vero Beach Airport (KVRB) ASOS.
An offshore moving thunderstorm continued to produce strong wind gusts, up to 34 knots at the Vero Beach Airport ASOS (KVRB).
An offshore moving thunderstorm produced a peak wind gust of 47 knots at the Ft. Pierce Airport (KFPR).
An offshore moving thunderstorm continued to produce high winds, up to 39 knots at the Ft. Pierce Airport (KFPR).

A funnel cloud developed along a line of low-topped showers in eastern Okeechobee County. These showers occurred along a sea and lake breeze convergence boundary on the northeast side of Lake Okeechobee. The funnel cloud lasted about 7 minutes, and was located around 3 miles east-northeast of the city of Okeechobee, Florida.

Police and SKYWARN reports, along with radar data, indicate that a cluster of slow eastward moving thunderstorms produced strong downburst winds which resulted in some minor damage in Palm Bay. An aluminum carport was blown across the road near the intersection of Fears Road SE and San Fillippo Drive. Nearby, signs were blow over at a construction site, resulting in minor injuries to one individual near the intersection of Cogan Drive SE and Toluca Street.
A severe thunderstorm downed many large tree limbs in the Tosohatchee Wildlife Management Area in Orange County south of Highway 50 near the town of Christmas.
A funnel cloud was observed over Patrick Air Force Base, moving east. The public report was relayed via an Orlando TV Station.
A funnel cloud was sighted near the intersection of Highway 520 and 528 by a Florida Department of Transportation crew.
Nickel sized hail was reported during a strong thunderstorm near the intersection of Barton Street and Dover Road in the town of Mims.

A weather spotter observed nickel size hail during an isolated strong thunderstorm which developed along an inland moving sea breeze boundary. The hail fell near the intersection of Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Darwin Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.

A cluster of strong thunderstorms developed east of Orlando and moved toward the coast. As the storms reached the border of Brevard County, they intersected an inland moving sea breeze boundary and briefly intensified to severe levels. Winds blew off a piece of a roof from a home and damaged a fence on Pine Street in Canaveral Groves. Nearby, a power pole was blown down onto a tree, downing powerlines toward the ground. The damage was reported near the intersection of Scarlet Avenue and Pine Street.

A peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at Patrick Air Force Base as a strong thunderstorm briefly and locally became severe before moving offshore. Along Highway A1A just east of the airbase, several hanging traffic signals were damaged.
A trained weather spotter observed a short-lived funnel cloud as an isolated thunderstorm developed along the sea breeze boundary.

Large hail, quarter to half dollar size, fell across portions of St. Cloud as a boundary induced severe thunderstorm moved northward at 10 to 15 mph. The falling hail was video-taped and submitted to an Orlando TV station. The video clearly showed large hail on the ground.

A large oak tree was downed due to severe thunderstorm winds near the intersection of 16th Street and Vermont Avenue in St. Cloud within Osceola County. The falling tree took out one or more power lines.

Strong rip currents occurred along the east central Florida beaches, peaking several days earlier due primarily to a swell propagating into the waters. The swell and resultant rip currents were lessening by May 31, however there were many swimmers in the water due to the Memorial Day weekend holiday. A local man was pulled from the surf at Paradise Beach Park in Satellite Beach and was given CPR, but he did not survive. Life guards were flying rip current flags and 22 rip current rescues were made within Brevard County this day.

A trained weather spotter reported numerous large tree limbs downed as a severe storm passed over the region. The strong winds were causing the limbs to become projectiles as they remained suspended in the air. The damage occurred along Industrial 25th Street in Ft. Pierce.

A storm spotter, a mariner and the general public observed and reported a funnel cloud occurring over the Banana River, just northwest of Port Canaveral. One or possibly two funnel clouds lasted a total of about 20 minutes and moved little during the period. The funnel was associated with an isolated heavy shower which developed along the east coast sea breeze boundary.
A State Emergency Manager observed nickel size hail near the intersection of John Young Parkway and Orange Blossom Trail in Orlando during a strong thunderstorm.

Two isolated thunderstorms merged over Geneva and likely produced severe, but localized downburst winds. A Division of Forestry official reported five oak trees toppled and uprooted adjacent to the St. Johns River in Geneva.

Lightning associated with a strong thunderstorm struck a large estate home in the Sweetwater Club subdivision of Longwood. The home became fully engulfed in flames and officials declared it a total loss.
A strong thunderstorm became locally severe, with winds uprooting multiple large trees in Audubon Park within Orlando. Numerous power lines were also downed.

Two thunderstorms merged over St. Cloud and the resultant storm produced a locally damaging microburst. The microburst winds uprooted four trees with diameters of 17 to 24 inches, north of Highway 192 and east of Narcoossee Road. A shed was also damaged on the property.

A funnel cloud was reported near the intersection of Highway 60 and Interstate 95, west of Vero Beach by several individuals, including a County Sheriff, pilot, Vero Beach Weather Observer and the public. A storm chaser video-taped a brief tornado touchdown in association with the funnel cloud. Radar imagery indicated that the tornado was a landspout which formed as an outflow boundary from strong convection farther west intersected a newly developed storm to the east of the main convection. The tornado touched down in a rural area and no damage occurred.

Sea breeze boundaries collided and produced a severe thunderstorm which damaged several mobile homes within the Colonial Village Mobile Home Park in Orlando. The winds downed several trees, damaged siding and gutters on several mobile homes and destroyed a car port.

Colliding sea breeze boundaries created a locally severe thunderstorm whose winds toppled a tree onto a mobile home in the Palm Valley Mobile Home Park in Oviedo. A young boy in the home experienced minor injuries to his arm as a result of the falling tree.
Severe thunderstorm winds knocked down several 20 to 40 foot tall trees. Minor damage to a fence also occurred.
Penny sized hail was observed during a thunderstorm, near the intersection of Dean Road and University Boulevard by a citizen.

The waterspout lasted only 60 to 90 seconds. Photographs verified the waterspout. The waterspout formed in association with an isolated shower along a sea-breeze boundary and ahead of a line of approaching thunderstorms.

As a line of thunderstorms moved from the mainland to the Volusia County coast, a|waterspout formed over Browns Bay, a marshy area east of the intracoastal river. The waterspout moved onshore the adjacent barrier island in New Smyrna Beach and produced minor damage as it crossed to the Atlantic coast. Six homes received minor damage, and one home experienced more extensive damage as a small part of roofing plywood and shingles was removed. Insulation was blown to the ocean about a half mile away. See separate waterspout entry.

A waterspout developed over the intracoastal waterway and moved onshore and inland for a short distance before dissipating as the circulation approached US Highway 1. The waterspout developed in association with an isolated, heavy shower that peaked in intensity near the time of the touchdown. The waterspout moved onshore the mainland as a very weak tornado and first impacted Cameron's Marina, where a small boat on a trailer was overturned, damaging an adjacent pickup truck. The weak tornado then continued moving inland on a northwest track, causing soffit damage to another residence and minor tree damage along the remainder of the path. The waterspout/tornado was observed and photographed by many individuals. Interestingly, a condensation funnel was not visible throughout its short life cycle, however, swirling water and debris were apparent and were lifted far aloft. See separate event for waterspout.

Volusia County EVAC Ambulance personnel reported a tornado touchdown in a heavily wooded area just west of Interstate 95 and south of State Road 44 in rural Volusia County to the west of New Smyrna Beach. The brief tornado touchdown occurred along the southwest edge of a cluster of strong thunderstorms which were training slowly northward.

events.cz_name: FLAGLER BEACH TO VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE 0-20NM
events.event_narrative: An isolated heavy shower developed near the Volusia County coast and moved inland to the intracoastal waterway. A waterspout formed near the shower, then moved ashore the mainland as a tornado. A condensation funnel was not present, however observers viewed and photographed a significant area of rotating water/spray picked up from the river surface. See the separate tornado entry for further information.

Frequent to excessive cloud to ground lightning erupted within a cluster of storms over western Orange County between 1530 and 1600 LST. During the next two hours, three homes in Windermere caught fire due to earlier lightning strikes. The first house, damaged by fire, was reported at 1644 LST. One fireman sustained minor indirect injuries due to smoke inhalation while fighting the fire. At 1652 LST, a fire was reported within a large estate home. The fire destroyed the home. A third house fire was reported nearby at 1740 LST and this home was damaged by fire. The following day, shortly before 0900 LST and 15 hours after the lightning storm, another estate home in Windermere caught fire and was destroyed. Fire officials believed that lightning from storms the previous afternoon struck the house and smoldered overnight. One fireman was treated for smoke inhalation while fighting this fire, an indirect, minor injury related to the lightning strike.

Weather likely played an indirect role in a vehicle-related fatality in DeLand. Saturated ground existed across the area due to several previous days of localized heavy rainfall. Between 1400 and 1500 LST, a thunderstorm moved southwest across DeLand, resulting in a quick two inches of additional rain and wind gusts to around 30 mph. These conditions combined with the pre-existing saturated ground, likely weakened and helped topple a large pine tree. A moving pickup truck was hit by the falling tree, then ran off the shoulder of the road as the driver lost control.  The woman passenger was killed and the driver, her husband, was critically injured.

A man drowned off Seagull Park in Satellite Beach at 1350 LST August 28, while surfing within the high surf associated with distant Hurricane Danielle. Indications are that the surfer was hit on the head by his surf board as a result of successive 4 to 6 foot swells, and subsequently drowned. Life guards rescued nearly 100 people from the beaches of Brevard and Volusia Counties on August 28 alone. The high surf and dangerous rip currents persisted for several days.
A trained storm spotter observed funnel cloud formation over rural Lake County, about 10 miles northwest of his location.
Lightning from a strong storm over Windermere struck a home and caused a fire which destroyed the home. Two firemen were treated for smoke inhalation while fighting the fire.

An isolated early evening thunderstorm developed just south of Wekiva High School, where a football game was underway. School officials suspended the game and asked spectators to evacuate the stadium. As the stadium was being cleared, lightning struck one of four towering light posts and two people were injured (one person was leaning against a metal fence adjacent to the stands). Both individuals were transported to the hospital and were later released.

A weather spotter observed formation of a funnel cloud a few miles south of his location along highway 60. The funnel persisted about 10 minutes and was photographed. Weather radar did not indicate any showers or storms in the area. The fair weather funnel cloud likely formed along a small-scale cloud boundary.

An EF0 tornado touched down just east of Interstate 95 in the town of Viera in central Brevard County and remained on the ground for over 7 miles, then exited into the Atlantic. The tornado moved from the mainland, across the Indian River, to Merritt Island, then across the Banana River to the beach-side barrier island between Patrick Air Force Base and Cocoa Beach, then exited into the Atlantic. One hundred and forty three homes sustained minor damage in Viera, mainly damaged/destroyed screen pool enclosures, damage to soffits, gutters and some shingles. Minor damage to six homes occurred on Merritt Island and four apartment units and several vehicles in Cocoa Beach. Numerous trees were toppled or snapped along the entire swath of damage. One person was slightly injured in Viera due to flying debris/glass. EF assessment: DI2, DOD2, LB-EXP.

Three guests on the restaurant patio and five water park staff nearby at an adjacent photo shop were indirectly struck and sustained minor injuries. All persons were examined, treated, and released from local hospitals and urgent care centers.

The current from the lightning strike reportedly passed through the water, went through the boat's motor, metal steering cables and into the wheel that the man held. A storm sparked by the collision of the east and west coast sea breezes over Lake County spawned a waterspout over Lake Eustis.  The waterspout moved onshore the north shore of Lake Eustis into the Grand Island area and caused damage to three residences.  A boathouse roof was blown away on one property, a screen porch was destroyed with some water intrusion inside the home on a second property, and a third residence had sheets of plywood blown away, causing some water intrusion into the house. Scattered showers and thunderstorms formed out in front of the inland-propagating east coast sea breeze.  A citizen observed a funnel cloud produced by one of the thunderstorms near the Orlando International Airport. The person viewing the funnel cloud reported that it did not touch down.

A citizen observed a funnel cloud briefly touch down in a mostly vacant lot near the intersection of Highway 50 and Highway 417 in Orlando. The landspout tornado picked up some sand and dust, which was lifted aloft within a debris cloud. The touchdown lasted between 30 and 60 seconds and resulted in no damage. Observations from three nearby construction workers suggest the winds were well below severe limits (estimated at only 30-35 mph).

Several public reports of a short-lived funnel cloud were received from near Lady Lake. Multiple photos were obtained and showed that the funnel cloud did not come in contact with the ground. No injuries or damage occurred.

Radar-detected rotation within a northeastward moving thunderstorm cell spawned a short-track EF0 tornado in Vero Beach Highlands. A NWS damage survey estimated maximum winds of 65-70 mph. An unoccupied home on 22nd Place SE sustained major damage, with part of the roof removed. A metal storage shed on a nearby property became airborne and landed in a neighbors front yard. Small branches broke from trees and shrubs were knocked down within a and light damage (mainly to soffits and due to impact from debris) occurred to other homes within the area. There were no injuries.  ||Light damage extending one block north and south of 22nd place southeast with small trees damaged and metal storage shed blown off its foundation.

A thunderstorm quickly intensified southwest of Indiantown and produced a brief, but high-end EF0 tornado in rural area north of the town center. A NWS damage survey estimated maximum winds of 80-85 mph. The tornado caused mainly light damage to a two-story home (several windows blown in, vinyl siding removed, soffit damaged), caused the roof of a pole barn to collapse upon itself, and totally removed the roof of an adjacent commercial building (VFW lodge). Several large tree branches were downed and one tall pine tree was uprooted. DI1 DOD5 LB, DI2 DOD2 EXP, DOD28 DI3 EXP.

A NWS Storm Survey team confirmed a brief touchdown of an EF0 tornado within the Ridgeway Mobile Home Park in Hobe Sound. Winds were estimated at 65 to 70 mph. The tornado removed the roof from one mobile home and carried it approximately 50 yards downwind. Small portions of metal roofs were peeled back from three other mobile homes. Thirty eight additional mobile homes experienced minor damage to window awnings and carports. Two vehicles experienced damage due to movement by the wind into an adjacent structure. Three large palm trees were uprooted or toppled, and many smaller trees sustained damage. The tornado lifted just prior to reaching Highway A1A. DI3 DOD4 LB.

Three hour rainfall totals of 3.5 to nearly 6 inches producing localized flooding in Vero Beach. Water entered several homes in the Wood Lawn Mobile Home community as the rain overwhelmed the drainage pipes. Nearby, the Osceola Magnet School, located within a low-lying area, was inundated with water. Standing water also caused the temporary closure of several roads.

The cell which produced the Ridgeway Mobile Home Park tornado moments earlier, produced another brief EF0 tornado which impacted the Loblolly Bay residential community. The tornado toppled multiple trees, then likely moved over Peck Lake as a waterspout. Winds were estimated at 65 to 75 mph. A video of the circulation and debris was taken by a homeowner located one mile due south of the tornado.

As the waterspout traveled across Lake Peck, severe wind gusts were measured by a 40-foot, moored, marine vessel, along with the observation of rotating debris. Measured wind gusts at the top of a 55-foot mast reached 65 knots from the south, then quickly shifted to the north as the circulation passed. The wind broke a port hole on the vessel, and damaged canvas on four nearby boats.

events.event_narrative: The 1112 foot long Freedom of the Seas cruise ship departed Port Canaveral, Florida and traveled through convective bands on the west side of the gale/hybrid low. The anemometer (presumably at a height above 200 feet) measured wind gusts above 75 knots, with a peak wind of 90 knots. The ship was reported to have listed 12 degrees as it navigated the high winds and seas. Royal Caribbean Cruise Line reported 13 passengers experienced minor injuries due to severe ship movement. The ship sustained some damage to public areas and guest staterooms, but the sea-worthiness of the ship was not affected.

Heavy rainfall associated with training cells over several hours produced 5 to 10 inches across much of Osceola County. Heavy rainfall caused a stream extending from Lake Marian to flow over a roadway at the intersection of Lake Marian Road and Peavine Trail in rural southeastern Osceola County, resulting in a washout of the roadway. Other roadways were closed in St. Cloud due to high levels of standing water. Three day rainfall totals ending at 0600 EST October 10 reached as high as 16.79 inches at a cooperative observer site 8 miles west of Yeehaw Junction (YEHF1).

Weather spotters reported rainfall totals of 5-10 inches due to persistent heavy cells, leading to urban, small stream, and roadway flooding in the Suntree, Viera, and North Melbourne areas. Most of the heavy rain occurred from the early morning hours though mid evening, with 3-day rainfall totals ending at 0600 EST October 10 reaching as high as 12.08 inches at a CoCoRaHS rainfall observer site 4.3 miles north-northwest of Palm Shores (FL-BV-20).

Heavy rainfall associated with persistent cells produced urban, small stream, and roadway flooding in the Palm Bay area. The highest 3-day rainfall total reported within Brevard County, ending at 0600 EST October 10, was 14.82 inches, at a CoCoRaHS site located 1 mile northeast of Palm Bay (FL-BV-14).

Heavy rainfall associated with persistent cells produced urban, small stream, and roadway flooding in the Vero Beach area. Minor roadway and lowland flooding occurred within other parts of the county. The highest 3-day rainfall total reported within Indian River County, ending at 0600 EST October 10, was 15.55 inches, at a CoCoRaHS site located 4.8 miles west of Vero Beach (FL-IR-33).

Heavy rainfall associated with persistent cells produced urban, small stream, and roadway flooding in the Union Park area. Minor roadway and lowland flooding occurred within other parts of the county. The highest 3-day rainfall total reported within Orange County, ending at 0600 EST October 10, was 10.10 inches, at a CoCoRaHS site located 3.9 miles east of Union Park (FL-OR-9).

Gusty southeast winds created choppy two-to-three foot seas on the Indian River. A man fishing alone on the river within a 13-foot flat-bottom watercraft near Titusville was tossed from the boat by the rough seas and drowned. The man was not wearing a life jacket.

A spotter reported one foot of water flooded two roadway intersections to the southwest of Port Saint Lucie for a short period during the morning. Several other smaller streets were also closed due to periodic flooding throughout the day. More than 5 inches of rain were measured across much of St. Lucie County from early morning through mid evening, with reports ranging from Port Saint Lucie, east to the coast.

US Highway 1 was reduced to one lane for a short time during the morning as flooding impacted the remainder of the road. Several other nearby streets were also flooded and closed at times throughout the day due to persistent rain. Rainfall amounts of 5 to 8 inches were recorded throughout much of Martin County, from southwest of Palm City through Stuart, from the early morning hours through mid evening.

A brief tornado with estimated winds of 55 to 65 mph, or weak EF-0 strength, touched down in a rural, un-populated area east of U.S. Highway 441 and north of Highway 70, to the northeast of Okeechobee town. The touchdown was confirmed several days after it occurred, when the Florida Forest Service flew along the radar-based track of the storm. Sporadic wind damage was found along the storm track, consisting of isolated debris and vegetation blown-downs.

The first of three tornadoes associated with a Tropical Storm Debby mini-supercell that traveled from northern Okeechobee County to northern Brevard County occurred at Yeehaw Junction. The tornado touched down in a wooded area south-southwest of Highway 441, about 1 mile south of the State Road 60 intersection then traveled north for 3.1 miles, crossing Highway 441, State Road 60, and the Florida Turnpike. Considerable tree damage, mainly to pines and small brush occurred along the path. The tornado moved between the turnpike toll booth and an adjacent vacant motel, producing minor structural damage and downing trees. Debris impacted and damaged a parked car within the toll booth parking lot. One vehicle, driving on the turnpike, sustained damage from a falling tree. The damage location was also consistent with a very strong rotational signature, reflectivity hook echo and tornado debris signature on dual-pol radar data. DI28 DOD2 EXP, DI6 DOD2 LB.

The third and final tornado associated with a Tropical Storm Debby mini-supercell that traveled from northern Okeechobee County to northern Brevard County occurred just south of State Road 50 and west of Interstate 95, to the west of Titusville. This location was also just north of the Great Outdoors RV Park. Two motorists traveling on Highway 50 observed the tornado briefly touchdown (illuminated by lightning strikes), just to the south of their locations. One of the motorists provided a detailed eyewitness account of the tornado touchdown. While there was little to damage in the immediate area of the tornado, a path of downed tree limbs was noted immediately after the touchdown, from near the entrance of the RV Park to State Road 50.

The second of three tornadoes associated with a Tropical Storm Debby mini-supercell that traveled from northern Okeechobee County to northern Brevard County produced a short damage path through a wooded area within the Kempfer Ranch and Deseret Ranch in far eastern Osceola County, about 1 mile north of Highway 192. The damage path cut through an area of mainly pine trees, damaged a fence, and displaced a pile of aluminum pipes downstream. The damage location was also consistent with a very strong rotational signature, reflectivity hook echo and tornado debris signature on dual-pol radar data. An Osceola County Emergency Management Official surveyed the damage path and provided details and damage photos. DI28 DOD2 LB-EXP.

Tropical Storm Debby, located over the northeast Gulf of Mexico, created rough water conditions due to 20 mph winds with gusts to 35 mph. Two canoes went out on Lake Dorr with one adult in each canoe, and a total of five children divided between the two canoes. One canoe returned to shore to drop off the children, then attempted to return to the second canoe to assist them return to shore. While enroute, the canoe capsized and the person who was onboard drowned. The other canoe and occupant were helped back to shore by another vessel. None of the five canoeists were wearing life vests.

Several homes in the Indian Ridge Subdivision near Indian River Trail North in Kissimmee were impacted by high winds as a linear squall line associated with an outer rain band of Tropical Storm Debby (located over the northeast Gulf of Mexico) passed the area. One awning was ripped from a home and several small trees were downed. Three adjacent homes experienced significant damage to pool screen enclosures, and several other homes had minor damage to pool screen enclosures.

A mini-supercell traveled from Polk County to southeast Lake County and produced an EF0 tornado along a discontinuous path of 3.7 miles within Winter Garden in Lake County, just west of the Orange County line. The storm crossed Johns Lake, producing tornado damage on both the south and immediate north sides of the lake. Numerous trees were damaged as far south as Avalon Woods Drive, with four adjacent homes in the Suburban Shores Subdivision experiencing property damage on the northern end of the damage path. The damage consisted of large branches on a vehicle, a large tree on a roof of another home, and other homes with significant damage to pool screen enclosures. The supercell also produced a tornado nearly an hour earlier, well to the south in Polk County. DI28, DOD2, LB-EXP.

The very brief EF0 tornado impacted one condominium building within the Indian Pines Village. The tornado stripped several sections of plywood from one roof of a condo and another unit sustained a small hole in the roof and the front entrance awning was peeled back. An eyewitness within the condo village observed a funnel cloud to the west touch down and damage two condo units within the same building. After striking the condo units, roof debris was seen being lifted aloft and swirling. Roofing debris was carried eastward as the tornado quickly lifted. Debris fell to the ground and onto other condo roofs farther to the east-northeast. Debris also fell into a small pond just downstream, and into another pond and an adjacent wooded area at least 500 feet to the northeast. St. Lucie County Emergency Management assisted by surveying the damage and provided details of the event and damage photos. DI5 DOD2 LB.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread urban and lowland flooding across much of the county. Rainfall from the morning of August 26 until the evening of August 27 averaged 5 to 10 inches, with isolated totals of 12 to 14 inches, most of which fell during the morning and afternoon of August 27. The most significant impacts occurred in and near Jensen Beach, Stuart, Palm City, and Port Salerno. Several roads became temporarily impassible due to standing water. Water entered one complex in Palm City, comprised of multiple businesses.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread urban and lowland flooding across much of the county. Rainfall from the morning of August 26 until the evening of August 27 averaged 5 to 10 inches, with isolated totals of 12 to 14 inches, most of which fell during the morning and afternoon of August 27. The most significant impacts occurred near the coast, from Lakewood Park to Fort Pierce, White City, and Port St. Lucie. Numerous roads were temporarily closed due to standing water.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread urban and lowland flooding across much of the county. Rainfall from the morning of August 26 until the evening of August 27 averaged 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals of 14 to 17 inches, most of which fell during the morning and afternoon of August 27. The most significant impacts occurred near the coast from Winter Beach to Vero Beach and Florida Ridge. Twenty seven manufactured homes and two single family homes were damaged by water intrusion and 20 roads were temporarily closed due to standing water during the height of the flooding.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread urban and lowland flooding across much of the county. Rainfall from the morning of August 26 until the evening of August 27 averaged 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals of 10 to 14 inches, most of which fell from early morning until mid day on August 27. The most significant impacts occurred within the City of Okeechobee and adjacent rural locations, including Taylor Creek.  Fourteen homes experienced major damage and another 146 had minor water intrusion (from either leaking roofs and/or high levels of standing water, mainly from over-topping local creek/canals. Several roads were temporarily closed due to standing water.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced areas of urban and lowland flooding across portions of the county. Rainfall from the morning of August 26 until the evening of August 27 averaged 3 to 6 inches, with isolated higher totals, most of which fell during the morning and afternoon of August 27. The most |significant impacts occurred in St. Cloud and rural locations farther south and east. Several roads were temporarily closed due to standing water.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread flooding across the county. Rainfall totals from the morning of August 26 through late on August 27 averaged 5 to 10 inches, with isolated totals of 12 to 14 inches. Peak wind gusts reached 35-45 mph along the coast and shore of Lake Okeechobee.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread flooding across the county. Rainfall totals from the morning of August 26 through late on August 27 averaged 5 to 10 inches, with isolated totals of 12 to 14 inches. Peak wind gusts reached 35-45 mph along the coast.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread flooding across the county. Rainfall totals from the morning of August 26 through late on August 27 averaged 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals of 10 to 14 inches. One hundred and sixty homes sustained water damage, mostly minor, due to intrusion of standing water, mainly from over-topping of local creeks/canals. Peak wind gusts reached 30-40 mph along the shore of Lake Okeechobee.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced areas of flooding across portions of the county. Rainfall totals from the morning of August 26 through late on August 27 averaged 3 to 6 inches, with isolated higher totals. An EF-0 tornado occurred near St. Cloud and damaged several structures.

Persistent heavy rainbands from Tropical Storm Isaac produced widespread flooding across the county. Rainfall totals from the morning of August 26 through late on August 27 averaged 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals of 14 to 17 inches. Peak wind gusts reached 35-45 mph along the coast. An EF-0 tornado occurred in Vero Beach and damaged 95 structures (mostly mobile homes).

An EF-0 tornado, with winds estimated near 65 mph, touched down in rural St. Cloud and destroyed an old, abandoned mobile home (floor attachment to the frame was severely rotted), then continued across a wooded lot and open, old citrus groves, causing minor-moderate shingle damage to a block home (house window was broken from debris impact), and minor shrub and fence damage within the yard of a neaby home. Insulation and small debris from the mobile home was carried downstream throughout the distance of the track. DI3 DOD6 Below LB; DI2 DOD1 EXP; DI27 DOD1 EXP.
A South Florida Water Management District mesonet site along the Indian River in Port St. Lucie measured gusts to 37 knots as a thunderstorms passed offshore.
A weather spotter estimated wind gusts of 35 knots (and pea-sized hail) as a thunderstorm passed over Port Salerno and continued into the intracoastal and nearshore Atlantic waters.
A thunderstorm produced a peak wind gust of 45 knots from the west as the storm crossed the Vero Beach Airport (KVRB) and continued east across the intrcoastal and adjacent Atlantic waters.

A strong thunderstorm uprooted a large tree at the Indian River County jail. The ground was very moist from flooding a week earlier and likely contributed to the uprooting. A fence was damaged by the falling tree. Also at the jail, two law enforcement vehicles experienced minor damage after being impacted by debris. One vehicle was hit by a plastic chair and the other one was damaged when a wheeled storage trailer rolled into it. Measured wind gusts at the nearby Vero Beach airport reached 52 mph.

Several wooden power poles to the northeast of Okeechobee, near 7200 U.S. Highway 441 North, were tilted by severe thunderstorm winds, with the two poles experiencing broken cross members. While a funnel cloud was reported in the area (see separate event), the wind damage appeared to be due to straight line winds.
Okeechobee County Fire/Rescue relayed a public report of a funnel cloud near Okeechobee.

A 66-year old man visiting from Arizona was caught in a rip current in the Atlantic, near the Ocean Landings Resort and Racquet Club in Cocoa Beach. The man was pulled to shore by emergency personnel and was transported to the hospitial. He died, due to drowning, a short-time later. Several others people were rescued from rip currents during the weekend.

A mesonet site at Jensen Beach (XJEN) recorded sustained north winds of 39 mph. These winds impacted much of the Martin County barrier islands. Gusts of 50-55 mph occurred, especially during passing squalls.

Moderate to major beach erosion, with approximately 17 structures in danger or threatened by additional short-term erosion. Of these 17 structures, two were multi-family buildings and two were businesses. Seven of the sites experienced structural damage to the primary structure or to attached patios or pools. Several beach crossovers and lifeguard towers were also damaged, as well as a boat ramp.
Moderate to major beach erosion. Several beach crossovers and a lifeguard tower were damaged. Sea water and sand washed onto one coastal road.
Moderate to major beach erosion. Sand over-washed two beach access parking areas and erosion damaged the foundation of a pump station.

Moderate to major beach erosion. Erosion caused damage to two homes and washed sand and debris across a coastal roadway, temporarily isolating residents. Several piers, boardwalks and retaining walls were also damaged.

The tornado began at US Highway 1 in Edgewater and continued northeast through the Terra Mar Village Mobile Home Park to Alice Street and Jones Fish Camp Road, then moved onto the intracoastal river as a waterspout (see 1726 LST waterspout episode). A total of 62 homes were damaged (17 with minor damage and 45 with major damage), impacting carports, awnings, roofs, power poles and lines, and numerous trees. Over 100 trees (many very large) between the mobile home park and the intracoastal river were snapped near the ground or uprooted. Metal from the mobile homes were carried far downstream. The frame of a mobile home was wrapped several times around the base of a tree. The tornado produced high-end EF0 damage within the mobile home park, then strengthened to a high-end EF1 tornado with a widening damage swath along Jones Fish Camp Road and upon approach to the intracoastal waterway. There were two very minor injuries, both treated at the scene. Maximum winds estimated at 90-110 mph. A motorist travelling on US Highway 1 videotaped the tornado crossing the highway in front of him, with debris evident within the circulation as it reached the mobile home park. Several other citizens and a public safety official also witnessed the tornado. DI3 DOD4 EXP; DI3 DOD8 LB-EXP; DI27 DOD4 EXP; DI28 DOD4 EXP.

The tornado which impacted Edgewater from 1725-1726 LST, continued northeast across the intracoastal waterway (1726-1729 LST), then moved across the narrow barrier island at Bethune Beach as a small, weak tornado. Several power lines were downed by the tornado along Highway A1A and small debris from palm trees and shrubs were observed along the path. A citizen observed the tornado cross the barrier island, from the second story of his home just to the north. Maximum winds estimated at 55-65 mph.

A citizen videotaped a waterspout over Lake Apopka for several minutes as it moved northeast from near the center of the lake toward the northeast shore. A short time later, several citizens located a few miles northeast of the lake observed the waterspout move onshore and track across the rural Lake Apopka Restoration Area before dissipating.

Strong onshore (gradient) winds produced 6-8 foot seas near and offshore St. Lucie Inlet. A 23-foot commercial fishing boat was returning to port due to the rough conditions and capsized in the St. Lucie Inlet. A large wave pushed the boat forward and it then nose-dived into the back of another wave, ejecting four men from the vessel as it capsized. One man drowned and the other three were rescued by another commerical fisherman as they were hanging onto the overturned vessel.

She sustained a broken hip when a tree fell on her Florida room as she entered.

An EF0 tornado with winds estimated between 70 and 80 mph touched down near the Intersection of U.S. 1 and Dixon Boulevard in Cocoa and travelled northeast to the Indian River where it became a waterspout. Numerous trees were downed along Dixon Boulevard and Indian River Drive. DI27; DOD2; EXP, DI8; DOD2; EXP.

An EF0 tornado with winds estimated at 75 to 85 mph, affected primarily the Charolais Estates and Colfax Landing subdivisions in Viera/Rockledge. The damage damage was embedded within a larger swath of strong straight-line winds which affected areas extending farther to the west and east. Several homes experienced damage to roof tiles and soffits. Concrete roof tiles were carried downstream and penetrated several windows. Other metal debris was carried downstream and a fence was blown down. Numerous pool screen enclosures totally collapsed. DI2; DOD1; UB.

events.event_narrative: A short line of strong thunderstorms approached the Volusia County coast from the northwest, while an isolated storm approached from the southwest. As the storms interacted at New Smyrna Beach and spread offshore, southerly winds gusted to 36 knots at mesonet site DYTNB.

A NWS Storm Survey revealed an approximate three-quarter mile wide swath of straight-line thunderstorm wind damage extending 1.25 miles from Trimble Park to Lake Ola and Orange Blossom Trail in Tangerine. The damage consisted of mainly large trees toppled (most with extensive canopies), large tree branches downed and some fence damage. Very minor structural damage was noted to a few homes (chimney damage to two story homes). Maximum winds were estimated to be 70-80 mph.

A report was relayed of a sheriff deputy observing a funnel cloud in Eustis. The deputy confirmed the funnel cloud did not touch down.
A public report of a funnel cloud was received. The citizen estimated the location of the funnel cloud to be near I-4 in the Heathrow area.

Rainfall of 3 to 4 inches in a short period of time, associated with a strong thunderstorm, caused a steep 30 foot section of ground adjacent to State Road 50 in Clermont to slide into a home. The mudslide destroyed a home on Sunnyside Drive. Mud several feet high entered the home. The drainage system in the area was designed several decades ago and could not handle the excessive rain rate.

A 22 year old male tourist from New York became caught in a rip current and drowned. He was an inexperienced swimmer. Two others, a male and female, were also caught in the rip current, but were better swimmers and they escaped to safety. The nearest lifeguard tower was approximately 5 miles away.
A weather spotter observed three funnel clouds over Hutchinson Island, moving offshore.

An isolated thunderstorm produced a microburst which caused a few large trees to uproot, downed several large tree limbs and damaged two pool screen enclosures. One of the screen enclosures was damaged after a tree fell onto it.

A gustnado formed along an outflow boundary ahead of a weakening line of thunderstorms approaching the coast. The gustnado developed on Cocoa Beach, adjacent to the Coconuts on the Beach restaurant. The circulation lifted dozens of beach umbrellas and other objects at least 100 feet into the sky. Although the event only lasted about 30 seconds, the beach was highly populated and debris struck several people, resulting in injuries. Although most injuries were minor, a 15-year old boy suffered a head injury after being struck by a flying canopy, and was transported by ambulance to an area hospital.

events.cz_name: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
events.event_narrative: A gustnado formed on Cocoa Beach along an outflow boundary. The gustando only lasted about 30 seconds, but produced winds estimated near 40 knots as it travelled from the beach to the adjacent Atlantic, then dissipated. The circulation lofted dozens of beach umbrellas and other debris up to 100 feet into the air and carried them downstream over the Atlantic.

The front portion of the van then burst into flames. The driver was able to get out of the vehicle safely, with no injuries.
Heavy rain produced flooding of multiple streets in Deland, with several cars becoming stranded due to high water.
Heavy rain caused water to enter one home through its front door and garage in Deltona.

FAA officials in the control tower at Witham Field in Ft. Pierce observed a funnel cloud develop to the southeast over the Atlantic and touch down as a waterspout.The waterspout persisted for approximately 6 minutes off Sailfish Point before dissipating. The report was relayed by Martin County Fire Rescue.

A storm spotter reported a funnel cloud visible just north of Prima Vista Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. The duration of the funnel was only one minute and its formation occurred near an isolated thunderstorm.

A southward moving thunderstorm became severe and produced damaging microburst winds, estimated near 65 mph, impacting State Road 528, just west of the intersection with State Road 520 in rural, southeastern Orange County. Motorists driving eastbound on State Road 528 experienced sudden gusts of swirling winds along the leading edge of the microburst, which lofted dirt and small debris tens of feet into the air. Numerous branches were downed in the area and at least one tree was toppled and fell onto State Road 528.

events.event_narrative: An off-duty US Air Force weather observer spotted a funnel cloud developing over the Atlantic to the east of Patrick Air Force Base. A few minutes later, the funnel  became a waterspout. The waterspout moved toward shore but dissipated prior to reaching the coast.

An isolated heavy shower moved onshore from the Atlantic and produced very localized wind damage to an apartment complex. The strong winds ripped down a large section of siding from the second story of an apartment. No other damage was confirmed in the area.

A 23-year old male tourist in the surf zone about 100 feet offshore Cape Canaveral appeared to be in distress and was not able to swim. Lifeguards observed rip currents where the man was last seen. The body was recovered nearby about two hours later. An autopsy indicated the man had drowned.
A weather spotter observed a brief funnel cloud in association with a thunderstorm to the west of Vero Beach, approximately two miles west of Interstate 95.

Strong winds, estimated as sub-severe by fire department officials at the damage scene, downed an old tree, damaging a car, powerlines and a fence in Deltona. Nearby in Osteen, tree limbs were downed by the strong winds at the same time,  resulting in a briefly closure of the roadway.

A NWS Storm Survey confirmed a zone of straight-line wind damage approximately aligned northeast to southwest, approximately one-third of a mile long and up to about 300 feet wide, affecting the Woodbridge Mobile Home park in the town of Hobe Sound. Twenty mobile homes sustained wind damage. Carports and awnings were removed from homes, and several homes had parts of their metal roofs peeled back. Two large trees sustained damage, primarily from debris impact. Damage estimates totalled $150,000.

Radar-based rainfall estimates were between 6 and 12 inches across eastern-most St. Lucie County, with most of the rain falling in a 6-hour or less period. The twenty-four hour rain gage total at Ft. Pierce was 10.64 inches, but with most of the rain falling in less than 6 hours. Flooding closed many roadways, stranding vehicles. Drainage canals and creeks overflowed. While high water surrounded many subdivisions, businesses and homes, water was only reported to have entered one apartment complex in Ft. Pierce (three separate buildings). Damage estimated totalled over 20,000 dollars.

Radar-based rainfall estimates were between 6 and 12 inches across eastern-most Martin County, with most of the rain falling in a 6-hour or less period. The twenty-four hour rain gage total at Stuart was 10.55 inches and 12.00 inches at Nettles Island, but with most of the rain falling in less than 6 hours. Flooding closed many roadways, stranding vehicles. Drainage canals and creeks overflowed. While high water surrounded many subdivisions, businesses and homes, water only entered one building, a Martin County High School, causing an estimated $220,000 in damage.

A bow echo associated with a severe thunderstorm travelled rapidly east across southern Orange County. A NWS Storm Survey revealed an 8-mile long swath of straight-line (west-to-east) damage to trees, fences and signs. The width of the corridor of winds estimated between 45 and 60 mph varied between one-half mile and one-mile. Several homes and vehicles were damaged due to falling trees and tree branches.

A book-end vortex rapidly developed at the northern edge of a bow echo. A NWS Storm Survey confirmed an EF-0 tornado, with estimated ground-level winds of 65-75 mph. The tornado developed at the east edge of Lake Mary Jane (possibly beginning as a waterspout over the lake) and was embedded within a larger region of strong straight-line winds. The tornado impacted three blocks of homes in the Isle of Pines subdivision, then continued into a rural, unpopulated area farther east/northeast. While the homes sustained little direct structural damage from the winds, falling trees damaged several homes and vehicles along the tornado path. Winds at tree top level (50-100 feet above ground level) were estimated at 80-90 mph. Velocity data from the TMCO Orlando International Airport TDWR radar showed winds up of 100 mph at 300 feet above ground level. DI28 DOD 3 LB; DI2 DOD 1 EXP.
Several public reports of hail in Sanford up to the size of quarters was reported via social media.

As the squall line crossed southern Brevard County, damaging winds affected portions of Melbourne and Palm Bay and produced minor wind damage. Broadcast media relayed a photo of damage to the metal roof of a mobile home in the Lakewood Village subdivision in Melbourne. Two blocks away, a small portion of a roof on a single family home was peeled back. Power lines were downed from severe thunderstorm winds on Palm Bay Road west of Interstate 95.

A tornado touched down and reached maximum intensity (estimated 100-105 mph) within the Massey Ranch Airpark in Edgewater where three small aircraft were flipped and damaged and three large hangars sustained major structural damage. Several people were inside the hangars at the time, but were uninjured. The tornado continued northeast and uprooted or damaged many trees, caused minor damage to the roofs of several homes and destroyed sheds within the adjacent Wildwood neighborhood. Roof damage to several of the homes was due to falling trees. Several cars were damaged after being impacted by debris. Farther downstream, sporadic, less significant tree damage occurred. The tornado lifted near the Halifax River, approximately 1.7 miles from where it touched down. Property damage was estimated at $723,000, excluding damage to the aircraft. DI21 DOD3 EXP-UB.

events.event_narrative: Winds estimated at 35 knots following the passage of a thunderstorm outflow boundary produced a rapid steepening of waves on the Indian River, just north of the Eau Gallie in Indian Harbour Beach. Waves estimated near three feet capsized an 18-foot boat with six occupants midway between the causeway and Dragon Point at the south end of Merritt Island. A four year old boy and elderly woman became trapped underneath the boat and died after being transported to a nearby hospital. The other four people were pulled from the water by rescuers and transported to the hospital, then released. All onboard the boat were wearing life jackets.

events.event_narrative: Brevard County Fire Rescue and a storm spotter sighted a waterspout on the Indian River Lagoon east of the intersection of Olmstead Drive and US Highway 1 in Mims. The waterspout lasted approximately 20 minutes and had little apparent motion.
A citizen reported a funnel cloud approximately five miles west southwest of Lakewood park, moving east. The funnel cloud was associated with a thunderstorm.
FAA personnel at Kissimmee Airport (KISM) observed a funnel cloud west of the airport, moving south. The funnel cloud was associated with a thunderstorm.

A persistent area of thunderstorms produced 3 to 6 inches of rain in less than two hours across West Melbourne and Palm Bay. Many roadways become temporarily impassable and a van became stuck in a rain-filled median on Florida Avenue.

Rain totals of 4 to 7 inches accumulated in less than two hours due to persistent thunderstorms. Flooding of many roadways caused them to become temporarily impassable. Two county fire stations, and several homes and business became isolated due to high levels of standing water and some minor water damage was reported. The most impacted areas included Lake Mary, Casselberry, Ovideo, Winter Springs and Longwood.

Rain totals of 3 to 6 inches accumulated in less than two hours due to persistent thunderstorms. Flooding of several roadways caused them to become temporarily impassable. Several homes became isolated due to high levels of standing water. The most impacted areas included Winter Park, Azalea Park and Maitland.

A small area of persistent rainbands trained across New Smryna Beach during the late afternoon and early early evening. Rainfall totals reached 8 to 12 inches, resulting in significant urban and roadway flooding. Retention ponds and drainage canals overflowed and rising water entered 7 single family homes and one public building. Four of these structures experienced major damage, 3 had minor damage and one was affected. Estimated damage was over 500 thousand dollars. No injuries were reported.

A persistent area of heavy rain trained across Holly Hill, Daytona Beach, and Port Orange during the early morning hours until around sunrise. Rainfall totals reached 8 to 12 inches, resulting in significant urban and roadway flooding. Retention ponds and drainage canals overflowed and rising water entered 98 single family homes, 10 multi-family homes and 6 businesses. Thirty-five of these structures experienced minor damage and the remaining 79 were affected. Estimated damage was over 3 million dollars. No injuries were reported.

The ASOS at the Vero Beach Airport (KVRB) recorded wind gusts up to 37 knots as a strong thunderstorm moved northeast along the coast from St. Lucie County to Indian River County. The strong winds spread across the intracoastal waters near Vero Beach.

events.event_narrative: An off-duty NWS employee, fire/rescue personnel and a trained spotter reported a waterspout offshore Lori Wilson Beach Park in Cocoa Beach. The waterspout was associated with a shower along a cloud line. The waterspout moved west toward the coast, then dissipated just as it approached the beach.

The waterspout was the second one to form within the hour along a cloud line over the Atlantic and was associated with a moderate rain shower.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated near 60 mph produced damage to portions of the Merritt Island High School sport complex. The baseball field dugout was blown over and a portion of the football locker room awning was detached from the roof. A tennis court fence and baseball field center fence were also damaged.

Additional wind gusts to 35 knots and 34 knots were recorded at 1605 and 1610 EST respectively.
The Vero Beach ASOS (KVRB) reported a gust to 39 knots from the West-Northwest as storms associated with a squall line moved through.

events.cz_name: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
events.event_narrative: A Weatherflow station in the Banana River just north of the Merritt Island Causeway recorded a 46 knot wind gust from the west-southwest. Additional wind gusts in the vicinity during the time included a gust of 44 knots at USAF Wind Tower 9404 at 1610 EST, a gust of 34 knots at 1615 EST at a Weatherflow mesonet site on the Cocoa Beach Pier and a gust to 35 knots at the Patrick Air Force Base ASOS (KCOF).

A severe thunderstorm with estimated winds of 60 mph produced minor wind damage to a few mobile homes in the Lakeshore Landings community in Orlando. A porch was torn off one of the homes and flipped onto its roof. Several other homes sustained minor damage to soffits and siding, and several trees were damaged.

Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across Orange County during the day on the 25th, continuing into the 26th. Two day rainfall totals were 3 to 9 inches, with the highest totals across northern portions of the county including Winter Park, Union Park and Apopka.  Flooding of many roadways caused them to become temporarily impassable.

Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across much of Volusia County during the day on the 25th, continuing into the 26th. Two day rainfall totals were 4 to 8 inches, with the highest totals across coastal areas from Edgewater to Daytona Beach. These rainfall totals resulted in minor road flooding and closures along several streets in Edgewater, New Smyrna Beach and Daytona Beach. Minor flooding of three homes occurred in New Smyrna Beach, with estimated damage around 15 thousand dollars. No injuries were reported.

Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across Osceola County during the day on the 25th, continuing into the 26th. Two day rainfall totals were 4 to 7 inches, with the highest totals across the Four Corners area, as well as Holopaw and Deer Park. These amounts led to minor flooding of several roadways in the Holopaw area as well as overtopping a bridge near Deer Park.

A stretch of above normal temperatures led to favorable conditions for bathers and surfers at local beaches. Several rip current rescues occurred during this holiday vacation period. On Sunday, January 4 at 1600 EST, a 64 year old famous surf photographer from Rhode Island was upended by rough waves while surfing and knocked unconscious at Paradise Beach in Melbourne Beach.  He never regained consciousness and died about a week later in the hospital.

A strong cold front produced gale conditions in the Atlantic coastal waters on January 8 and caused seas to build to around 10 feet. Winds diminished the following day, but lingering swells continued to produce very rough surf conditions. A male surfer in his 60s was found unconscious and not breathing in the surf across from Patrick Air Force Base at 1045 EST. Bystanders returned him to shore, where a Patrick Air Force Base medical crew resuscitated him. He was transported to a local hospital in stable condition where he later recovered and was released.

Strong winds in association with a line of thunderstorms moved across St. Lucie County early Thursday morning. Straight line winds embedded in part of the line produced minor damage on Ulrich Road (between Oleander Avenue and US-1). Estimated winds of 50 to 60 mph produced damage to several large trees and one home sustained minor roof and soffit damage.
The ASOS at the Vero Beach Municipal Airport (KVRB) recorded a 42 knot wind gust out of the west as a strong thunderstorm moved offshore and into the intracoastal waterway.
The AWOS at Witham Field Airport in Stuart (KSUA) recorded a 37 knot gust out of the southwest as a line of thunderstorms moved over the airfield and offshore the mainland.
A SKYWARN spotter in The Vikings (also known at The Prairie) subdivision reported 10 to 15 minutes of small hail up to nickel sized associated with a strong storm moving over the area.

A slow moving strong storm across Okeechobee County produced 5 to 7 inches of rain across the northwest and central portions of the county during the afternoon and evening, primarily over the Kissimmee Prairie Preserve. The COOP observer at the Kissimmee Prairie Preserve reported 5.69 inches of rain in 24 hours while another range gauge at the park reported 6.92 inches. Most of this rainfall fell in less than 6 hours.||This heavy rainfall led to minor flooding of roadways across Central Okeechobee County. The Kissimmee Prairie observer reported several inches of standing water on local roadways, which remained passable.

A combination of CoCoRAaS, ham radio and public reports indicated 5 to 11 inches of rain fell across northeastern Martin County, with most of the rain falling in a 6-hour or less period. The highest totals occurred within the southwestern portion of Stuart and in Palm City. ||Flooding closed many roadways, stranding over 100 vehicles. Drainage canals and creeks overflowed. While high water surrounded many subdivisions, businesses and homes, water was reported to have entered 7 homes in Palm City. Damage was estimated around $105,000 dollars.

A combination of CoCoRaHS, ham radio, and public reports indicated 3 to 6 inches of rain fell across southeastern St. Lucie County, with most of the rain falling in a 6-hour or less period. ||Flooding closed many primary and secondary roadways, stranding and submerging many vehicles. Drainage canals and creeks overflowed. While high water surrounded many subdivisions, businesses and homes, no water was reported to have entered any homes or businesses.

A 17-year old male from the local area was swimming outside the guarded beach at Jaycee Beach Park in Vero Beach. Rip currents, rough surf and a south-to-north longshore current were present throughout the day. The swimmer was likely caught within a rip current around 1600 EST and drowned. His body was recovered in the surf south of Jaycee Beach Park two days later.

A tree fell on a carport and another fell on a home, briefly trapping an unknown number of people inside. At a nearby car dealership, several vehicles on display with their hoods raised sustained damage and several display windows were broken.

Multi-day rainfall totals reached 6-12 inches across much of eastern St. Lucie County. The highest measured rain gauge totals were 12.25 inches at the Nettles Island COOP site and 11.19 inches at Savannah Preserve. Temporary flooding of roadways, parking lots and yards occurred as retention ponds and drainage canals overflowed their banks. County Road 707 from Walton Road to the Martin County line was closed for several days due to washouts.

Multi-day rainfall totals reached 6-12 inches across much of eastern Martin County. The highest measured rain gauge totals were 8.49 inches near Hobe Sound and 8.01 inches at the Stuart COOP site. Temporary flooding of roadways, parking lots and yards occurred as retention ponds and drainage canals overflowed their banks.

Multi-day rainfall totals reached 5-10 inches across much of eastern Indian River County. The highest measured rain gauge total was 7.00 inches near Vero Beach. Temporary flooding of roadways, parking lots and yards occurred. Retention ponds and drainage canals became full or overflowed their banks.

A NWS storm survey team determined an EF-1 tornado touched down in Hobe Sound, just east of U.S. Highway 1, in a wooded area between SE Courtney Terrace and SE Highpoint Way. Numerous uprooted trees (convergent pattern) indicated peak winds near 90 mph. The tornado then moved east-northeast and weakened to EF-0 strength, affecting a three block area before lifting near the intercoastal waterway between SE Marina Bay Drive and SE Palm Street. Eight homes sustained minor damage due to falling trees and debris penetration of windows. Four vehicles were also damaged from falling trees and flying debris. DI28 DOD3 EXP.

A NWS storm survey confirmed straight-line winds estimated near 60 mph on Nova Road, south of State Road 520 in rural, southeast Orange County. A few pine trees were toppled and many large branches were downed along about a one-mile, north-to-south stretch of the roadway. Minor wind damage to smaller branches continued for about 2 miles northeast, crossing State Road 520 (wind estimated 45-55 mph).

events.cz_name: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
events.event_narrative: A mariner who departed Port Canaveral  in a 17-foot fishing boat during the early-morning hours was lost at sea and presumed drowned. It is likely that the boater left port in light winds and small seas, but quickly encountered north winds gusting to 20 knots and building seas of 4-5 feet just offshore. The unoccupied boat was found late at night, about 20 miles south of Port Canaveral.

An elderly man left a boat ramp and ventured onto Lake Beauclair, near the Orange/Lake County line, around 0730EST on a day with south winds near 20 knots with gusts to 30 knots. The unoccupied boat was found going in circles nearby, around 1045LST. The body of the boater was discovered under water, three days later, about 30 yards from shore.

Strong and gusty northwest winds developed immediately behind a cold front just after midnight. Wind gusts around 25 knots likely caused river conditions to quickly become choppy. A 42-foot houseboat on the Indian River in Melbourne crashed into the north side of the Eau Gallie Causeway around 0115LST, injuring two elderly occupants. Police and several citizens stabilized the vessels and the officers pulled the two people to safety. They were taken to a local hospital with minor injuries.
Several public reports were received of a funnel cloud in Vero Beach. Photos and video were also obtained.
The Vero Beach Airport ASOS (KVRB) recorded peak wind gusts of 37 knots as a strong thunderstorm crossed the coast and continued across the intracoastal and near-shore Atlantic waters.

A severe thunderstorm produced hail up to golf ball size at the Country Hills Estates, north of the City of Okeechobee. The hail was observed at Okeechobee County Fire Rescue Station 4 near the intersection of Highway 441 and NE 168th Street, and also by nearby residents. The hail reportedly fell for over 5 minutes, Video was obtained.

Several residents in far southeast Palm Bay reported hail up to quarter size as a severe thunderstorm affected the area. A little further east, near the Indian River in Grant, a trained weather spotter observed dime size hail. All reports indicated the hail lasted for up to 5 minutes.

A large tree fell onto a home on New York Avenue in Deland during a late night thunderstorm. A large limb crashed through the roof of the home and penetrated into a bathroom. Winds were estimated near 50 mph.

Several trees were toppled due to high winds as a bow echo moved across East Orlando, including the Lake Nona area. Peak winds were estimated near 60 mph. Observations from the nearby Orlando International ASOS and Kissimmee Airport ASOS recorded gusts to 51 mph and 53 mph, respectively.

Four homes in Cape Canaveral sustained structural damage due to high winds associated with a bow echo which developed over Orange County and moved rapidly east and offshore. One home lost half of its roofing material, resulting in heavy water damage inside. The area affected encompassed a one-by-one block area.

A 41-year old man was struck by lightning in Jonathan Dickinson State Park, south of Hobe Sound. The man was playing catch with his son in a grassy field when he was struck by lightning on the top of his head. He was transported to a hospital in critical condition and died on April 4.

A long lasting severe thunderstorm moved from Polk County into northwest Osceola County and dropped hail between quarter and golf ball size for over 10 minutes. The hail piled up to over a foot deep at the peak of the storm in portions of Poinciana. Some hail damage occurred to the siding of homes, pool screens, recreational vehicles and cars.

Public reports indicated roof damage to manufactured homes within the Cypress Cove Nudist Resort in Poinciana. About a mile southwest of Cypress Cove, roofing material lifted off homes, scattered pine trees were downed or leaning significantly and numerous fence panels were scattered about. Some of this debris caused damage to cars.

A trained weather spotter reported quarter size hail near Lezze Road and Shirley Shores Drive in Tavares as a severe thunderstorm moved east across the area. Multiple other public reports of quarter sized hail were also received.
A trained weather spotter observed dozens of trees snapped and uprooted near the Squirrel Point Subdivision in Tavares. Photos provided confirmed the wind damage.
Storm spotters and a retired NWS employee observed penny sized hail lasting one to two minutes in the Hunters Creek area, southwest of Orlando.

A 58 year old man from Indiana downed after he and his son were pulled offshore within a rip current. Life guards rescued the son, but were unable to save the father, who was found face down in the water about 300 yards from shore. The man was unresponsive when transported to a hospital and was pronounced dead shortly after arrival.

Three of the boaters drowned and the fourth one was found alive on a Stuart Beach the following morning. The survivor stated the boat was swamped by rough seas shortly after leaving port for the fishing trip. The boat filled up with water and sank below the surface.

The tornado traveled mainly southward for nearly a half mile. Approximately 15 homes experienced damage, mainly to their roofs. Numerous trees were snapped and several fences and pool enclosures were destroyed. The tornado was rated EF1, with estimated maximum winds of 80-90 mph. DI2, DOD4, LB-EXP.

The tornado touched down within the Road Runner Travel Park and traveled southeast for just over a half mile before lifting. The tornado toppled four RV's and produced mostly minor roof and awning damage to several mobile homes. Several trees were downed and one large tree was snapped several feet above ground level. Persistent thunderstorms produced extremely heavy rain within a short time period from southern areas of Ft. Pierce northward to beyond the Indian River County line. Pierce ASOS (KFPR) recorded a record 9.85 inches for the day and 8.53 inches accumulated in four hours (1300-1700LST).

At about 1530LST on May 29, lifeguards at Spessard Holland Beach in Melbourne Beach rescued a 53 year old man from a rip current and resuscitated him. The man was transported to a local hospital, where he died approximately two weeks later. The cause of death was drowning. At about the same time of the initial incident, another lifeguard rescued two swimmers caught in a nearby rip current and noticed a third person submerged. The body of the third victim, a 20 year old male from Kissimmee, was recovered a few hours later. An autopsy confirmed he died due to drowning.

A 62 year old man from North Carolina was caught in a rip current in Daytona Beach around 1000LST on May 30 and rescued by lifeguards, but became unconscious while being brought back to shore. Initial indications point to a stress-induced heart attack. He was taken to the hospital and pronounced dead. Since the exertion of fighting the rip current likely contributed to the heart attack, this death was recorded as a rip current fatality.

Emergency management officials surveyed an area of wind damage in southern, rural Winter Garden and provided observations and photos to the NWS. In addition, several citizens provided valuable data and at least one person reported seeing a funnel cloud to his south shortly before the onset of damage. A path of damage occurred from the northern portion of the Orange County National Golf Center grounds, northward for 1.5 miles, paralleling Highway 429, just to the east. Significant tree was noted along Porter Road, and along both sides of Hamlin Groves Trail. Over 100 trees were damaged along the path (falling in a convergent pattern), including dozens of pine trees which were snapped several feet above the ground and many others which were uprooted. The path continued northward where five newly built homes on Bowman Drive were damaged. A pool screen enclosure and fences were damaged and a few homes experienced soffit, window and air conditioning unit damage from flying debris. Some debris was carried just north of New Independence Parkway, with no significant damage noted farther north. A review of all available data strongly suggested the damage was a result of a short-track, EF-0 tornado, with maximum winds estimated at 80 to 85 mph. DI1, DOD1, UB; DI28, DOD3, EXP; DI28, DOD4, LB.

Emergency Management officials provided detailed wind damage reports which occurred along a 4.35 mile long south-to-north path from Fruitland Park to Lady Lake, parallel to and just west of U.S. Highway 441. The damage consisted mainly of downed trees, branches and powerlines, although two homes in Lady Lake sustained structural damage due to falling trees. The most significant damage occurred on the east side of the tornado track, due to the rapid storm motion of 60 mph. The discontinuous damage path began near the College Avenue and W Miller Street in Fruitland Park and ended in Lady Lake, about midway between the Recreation Plantation RV Resort and Highway 441.  A review of all available data suggests that the wind damage was likely the result of a EF-0 tornado (winds estimated 70-75 mph). Isolated tree damage south and north of the tornado track was likely due to strong straight-line winds associated with the cell. DI2, DOD1, EXP; DI27, DOD2, EXP; DI27, DOD3, LB.

An eyewitness report documented the onset of the tornado within the St. Sebastian River Preserve State Park, south of Micco Road and west of the town of Micco, in far southern Brevard County. Based on results from a NWS damage survey and other eyewitness reports (including photographs), the tornado moved in a northerly direction for approximately 3.5 miles before lifting south of Grant Road. The tornado was rated as an EF-0, with maximum winds estimated at 75-85 mph.||The discontinuous damage path occurred within a mostly rural area within the town of Grant-Valkaria, with damage to a two block area that included Orchid Tree Drive, Cottonwood Drive and Crepe Myrtle Drive. An RV at the south end of Cottonwood Drive was toppled onto its side and a large mango tree was uprooted. Farther north, toward the middle of Orchid Tree Drive, a single family home had a large patio enclosure destroyed. The patio was connected securely to the home, resulting in a large portion of the home's roof also being removed. Debris was carried downstream over 100 yards in a northwest direction. A few additional homes nearby experienced minor soft and shingle damage. Numerous large tree branches were downed or damaged throughout the neighborhood. DI2, DOD4 LB; DI3, DOD5 LB; DI27, DOD2, EXP.

Three to five inches of rain fell within metro Orlando in less than an hour due to a stationary thunderstorm. Numerous cars became stranded in water over a foot deep and required first responders to rescue at least five motorists in Pine Hills. The rush of water was so strong, it tore the front bumper off one car and nearly flipped it over. Six inches of water entered cars and the high water approached the front doors of businesses. Several major roadways were closed due to the high water. High water also flooded streets and drains overflowed at Lee Road and Interstate 4, and the intersection of Mills Avenue and Colonial Drive in Orlando.
