Multiple videos were obtained from the public which confirmed a weak tornado (landspout) briefly occurred just south of the 33rd Street Industrial Park, in the area of Interstate 4 and Mall-at-Millenia. The landspout-tornado quickly dissipated and no damage occurred.

A trained spotter observed a brief tornado (landspout) develop near Lake Ellenor, lasting approximately 30 to 45 seconds before dissipating. No damage occurred from this landspout-tornado. Video corroborated the visual observation.

A National Weather Service damage survey and numerous eyewitness reports, photographs and video confirmed a waterspout/tornado moved north along a 5.1 mile path from Lake Conway to Thornton Park. The peak intensity was estimated at 100-105 mph.||A waterspout initially formed on the west-central portion of Lake Conway at approximately 1820LST and traveled north, briefly coming onshore and crossing a narrow strip of land at Hoffner Avenue, then moving back over water, crossing Little Lake Conway. The waterspout then moved back onshore as a tornado at the south end of Ferncreek Avenue. The tornado nearly paralleled Ferncreek Avenue and Martin Street as it moved nearly due north, crossing State Road 408, and lifting at Lake Lawsona Park at approximately 1832LST.||Damage was continuous along a 5.1 mile swath with a width of 350-500 yards. As the tornado came onshore at Hoffner Avenue it briefly attained EF-1 intensity (peak winds estimated at 85-90 mph) resulting in severe damage to the roof of a lakefront home and numerous large trees were toppled. Damage along much of the remainder of the path was rated EF-0 (winds estimated 65-85 mph).||The EF-0 damage consisted generally of uprooted trees, toppled trees, and snapped large branches. Several large trees fell onto homes, causing significant damage mainly to roofs. Multiple vehicles were damaged due to downed trees and fallen large branches. ||The tornado reached peak intensity of EF-1 in the vicinity of Ferncreek Avenue, Lake Margaret Drive and Carmia Drive (estimated peak winds 100-105 mph). Several one story apartment buildings lost significant portions of their roofs.||There were no injuries or fatalities. The Orange��County Property Appraiser's Office reported 42 homes and businesses were damaged, totaling $955,748.

A National Weather Service damage survey confirmed straight-line winds estimated at 55-65 mph impacted the Daytona Flea and Farmers Market in Daytona Beach around 2115 LST. Damage consisted of the removal of a large portion of a corrugated roof, with metal roofing peeled back on several adjacent buildings. Roof debris was blown downwind 100 yards onto adjacent portions of Interstate 95, causing the roadway to be closed for several hours. No other damage was noted in the area and there were no injuries or fatalities.

Numerous eyewitness reports, photographs and video were received from trained spotters and the public of a large waterspout that developed on Lake Monroe, which then came onshore briefly along the north shore of the lake as a rapidly weakening tornado. The waterspout developed on Lake Monroe at approximately 1927 LST and quickly became large, reaching an estimated maximum width of approximately 200 yards. The slow-moving waterspout then reached the north side of the lake near the 860th block of Lakeshore Drive in Enterprise at approximately 1934 LST as a rapidly weakening EF-0 tornado. The tornado dissipated between Lakeshore Drive and Jacob Brock Avenue, just east of the Florida United Methodist Children's Home and west of Broadway Street. An eyewitness near the point of dissipation, initially observed the waterspout over the lake, then described a complete lull of wind, followed by a increase of winds from the opposite direction, suddenly becoming very strong. Based on this report, along with only minor damage to trees near the lakefront, peak winds were estimated between 45 and 55 mph.

Reports from trained spotters and the public in Grand Island indicated that straight-line winds estimated between 55-60 mph occurred at approximately 2010 LST. The damage began along the north shore of Lake Eustis where several medium to large tree branches were downed. Additional damage occurred on Bristol Circle and Ashley Court where several fences were blow over, small trees toppled, medium tree branches downed, and loose backyard items tossed into adjacent properties.
The public reported a waterspout east of Fort Pierce Inlet.

Martin County Fire Rescue and local broadcast media reported that two men were struck by lightning while fishing at Hobe Sound Beach. The lightning strike occurred at approximately 1530 LST, 200 yards north of a lifeguard tower. First responders arrived to find the two men injured and both were transported to local hospitals in critical conditions.
Multiple reports received from trained spotters of a funnel cloud that persisted for approximately 3 minutes near Lake Yale.

Numerous photos and videos from trained spotters showed a brief tornado touchdown in the Emeralda Marsh Conservation Area just north of Lisbon. The tornado was on the ground less than one minute west of Emeralda Island Road between Lake Griffith and Lake Yale. The tornado produced no damage as it was over a marsh.
A trained spotter reported a dissipating funnel cloud looking east towards Lake Dora from the intersection of County Road 473 and U.S. Highway 441.
Lake County Sheriff's Office relayed report from public of a funnel cloud moving toward Silver Lake near the intersection of County Road 44 and Radio Road in Leesburg.

Based on numerous videos, pictures, and reports received from Lake County Emergency Management, Lake County Sheriff's Office, local broadcast media, trained spotters and the public, a waterspout on Lake Dora came onshore in Tavares as a brief tornado before quickly dissipating. The waterspout formed on Lake Dora at approximately 1741 LST. The waterspout came onshore on the north side of the lake near the 32900th block of Lakeshore Drive in Tavares at approximately 1742 LST, as a weakening tornado. The tornado knocked down a power pole and transformer on Lakeshore Drive before dissipating north of the road. Peak winds are estimated between 60-65 mph. No other damages or injuries occurred.

Eyewitness reports indicated that a waterspout developed over Sykes Creek near a strong thunderstorm (however it was not raining at the time), then moved southeast and reached land less than a minute later. A NWS Storm Survey confirmed the circulation reached land toward the west end of Island Drive on North Merritt Island, where the strongest winds of the tornado occurred (EF-0, estimated winds 55-65 mph), removing a porch from the back yard of a home immediately adjacent to the creek. The tornado lifted the porch over the home and dropped it into the front yard. The tornado weakened as it traveled southeast for less than a half-mile, causing minor shingle, soffit and fence damage along it's short track.

A National Weather Service Damage Survey confirmed that a brief EF-0 tornado impacted the Sunset Hills subdivision east of Orange City. The tornado tracked along a 0.1 mile long path, with maximum winds estimated between 65-75 mph. The tornado had a maximum width of approximately 70 yards. Several large tree branches were downed on both sides of County Road 4101, between Sunnyside Ave and E Graves Ave. A mobile home was destroyed after its roof caved in at the intersection of Sunnyside Ave and County Road 4101. Preliminary damage estimates from the Volusia County Property Appraiser was $40,000, with one structure destroyed. There were no reported injuries or fatalities.

A National Weather Service Damage Survey confirmed that a strong tornado moved through North DeLand along a 4.6 mile long path with peak winds estimated between 110-120 mph. The tornado began around the intersection of W Minnesota Ave and N Ridgewood Ave, near the West Minnesota Estates neighborhood. The tornado generally tracked east-northeast across the city resulting in many downed medium to large tree branches, downed power lines, and numerous large trees were uprooted, which led to many local and major roadways being blocked. Many homes and vehicles suffered moderate to major damage as large tree branches or entire trees fell on them.||The tornado briefly intensified just southwest of the intersection of W Plymouth Avenue and N Spring Garden Avenue where EF-1 damage occurred. Two storage facility buildings suffered major roof collapse with winds estimated at 80-90 mph. The tornado continued to produce EF-0 damage along and south of W Plymouth Avenue as it moved towards Woodland Blvd. ||As the tornado reached Woodland Blvd. it quickly intensified and reached its widest point at approximately 550 yards. Extensive EF-1 damage was seen from Woodland Blvd. east to Amelia Avenue, and from E Kentucky Ave south to E Woodmont Road, with winds estimated between 90-100 mph. Damage was most significant along E Washington Ave between N Alabama Ave and N Amelia Ave, just east of US Hwy 17 where winds are estimated between 110-120 mph. Two homes had total roof loss, with a few others receiving moderate to major roof and structural damage. Several healthy tree trunks were found snapped and twisted near the base, with numerous smaller trees snapped midway. Videos taken along N Woodland Blvd revealed that a box delivery truck was tipped over and a car was flipped.||The tornado dissipated just east of the Lake Lindley subdivision between Jacobs Road and Lake Talmadge Drive where many large branches were snapped near the tops of the trees. ||There was one injury and no fatalities reported. Preliminary damage estimates from the Volusia County Property Appraiser indicate total damage of approximately $8,010,339. There were 163 damaged structures, with 49 sustaining minor damage, 40 sustaining major damage, and 5 that were destroyed.

In Volusia County, wind gusts to tropical storm force in squalls occurred only along the immediate coast and for a short duration. Sustained winds in Volusia County remained below tropical storm force as the center of Isaias remained far away to the east. The highest sustained wind was measured at New Smyrna Beach (36 mph from the north at 0127LST on August 3), and the peak wind gust was also at New Smyrna Beach (41 mph from the north at 0124LST on August 3).

In Martin County, sustained tropical storm force winds affected the barrier islands, with gusts to tropical storm force in squalls through much of the remainder of the county from early morning through late afternoon August 2. The highest sustained wind was measured at House of Refuge in Stuart (48 mph from the east at 0654LST on August 2) and the peak gust was also House of Refuge in Stuart (52 mph from the east at 0733LST on August 2).

In Saint Lucie County, sustained tropical storm force winds affected the barrier islands, with gusts to tropical storm force in squalls through much of the remainder of the county from early morning through late afternoon August 2. The highest sustained wind was measured at the Saint Lucie Nuclear Power Plant (41 mph from the northeast at 0705LST on August 2), and the peak gust was also at the Saint Lucie Nuclear Power Plant (46 mph from the northeast at 0705LST on August 2).

In Indian River County, sustained tropical storm force winds affected the barrier islands, with gusts to tropical storm force in squalls through much of the remainder of the county from mid morning through early evening August 2. The highest sustained wind was measured at Indian River Shores (40 mph from the north-northeast at 1317LST on August 2) and the peak gust was also at Indian River Shores (50 mph from the northeast at 1224LST on August 2).

In Brevard County, sustained tropical storm force winds affected the barrier islands, with gusts to tropical storm force in squalls through much of the remainder of the county from late morning through very early morning August 3. The highest sustained wind was measured at US Air Force Wind Tower 0002 in Cape Canaveral (47 mph from the north-northeast at 2322LST on August 2) and the peak gust was at US Air Force Wind Tower 0108 in Cape Canaveral (53 mph from the northeast at 2000LST on August 2).

The roof collapsed on the sheriff annex building. Several hangers were damaged. The storm also knocked out power to 10,000 power company customers  in the arera. The local YMCA had minor roof damage as well as a building at the fairgrounds.

Several trained weather spotters and citizens observed development of a funnel cloud over Lake Tohopekaliga (Toho) in Kissimmee. The funnel cloud extended to the lake and became a brief waterspout toward the southwest portion of the lake, while moving little. A light shower was in the vicinity, with stronger thunderstorms farther east. The waterspout was visible from the northeast (St. Cloud) and from the west and southwest (Kissimmee). Multiple photographs and videos helped document the waterspout.

Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding occurred near the times of high tide. The greatest impacts were reported along portions of Daytona Beach, New Smyrna Beach and Bethune Beach. Dunes, jetties and seawalls were overwashed, with water over several beachfront roads, requiring closures. Beach erosion was primarily minor to moderate, with flattening of the beach profile and dune recession ranging from none to moderate.

Local, minor coastal flooding occurred near the times of high tide. The greatest impacts were reported along Melbourne Beach, where several county crossovers were damaged. Minor to moderate beach erosion occurred along the central and northern county beaches, with moderate to severe erosion along the south county beaches (Spessard Holland Park to Sebastian Inlet State Park). The tallest dune escarpment within this area was about 12 feet.

Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding occurred near the times of high tide. The greatest impacts were reported near Ft. Pierce Inlet, where the boat launch was closed due to missing planks on a dock and some washouts nearby. In addition, the earthen berns surrounding several mosquito impoundments along both sides of the Indian River |suffered minor erosion from overwash. Beach erosion was mainly minor, except locally moderate along portions of Ft. Pierce Beach, where about 30 feet of beachfront was lost.

Minor to moderate coastal flooding occurred near the times of high tide. The greatest impacts occurred as excess sea water entered St. Lucie Inlet and raised water levels within the St. Lucie River. Water inundated many roadways and properties adjacent to and near the river, primarily within Palm City, Stuart, Sewall's Point and Port Salerno. High water levels within the Indian River caused roadway flooding in Jensen Beach, as well as roadway flooding and water intrusion into a few homes in Hobe Sound. Sea water also entered Jupiter Inlet and raised water levels within the Indian River and Loxahatchee River, causing roadway flooding in far south Jupiter Island and in Tequesta. Beach erosion was primarily minor to locally moderate.

Minor to locally moderate beach erosion impacted the Indian River County beaches. The most significant erosion occurred at Jaycee/Conn Beach near Vero Beach, where several feet of berm lowering was observed, with one foot of dune retreat. Moderate erosion was also observed at Wabasso Beach and Tracking Station Beach.

Local broadcast media relayed a report and photograph of a well-defined funnel cloud over a lake in Windermere. The photograph hinted that the funnel cloud may have briefly formed into a waterspout on an inland lake, but this could not be confirmed.

A 27-year old man from Ocala, Florida was swimming in rough surf with other family members at an unguarded portion of Daytona Beach during the early afternoon, when they got caught in a rip current. All family members except the 27-year old man returned safety to shore. The man disappeared in the surf and his body was recovered the following day about nine miles north of where he went missing. He died from drowning, after being caught in the rip current.

He was rescued from the water, but was unresponsive. He was transported to a hospital, but later died on October 9, with drowning the cause of death.

Between 5 and 8 inches of rain fell during the early morning hours, within an area with a shallow water table due to previous heavy rainfall. Showers moved onshore or developed along the coast and trained over areas south of Port Salerno, impacting Hobe Sound most significantly, and in particular Hobe Heights. Rapid inundation occurred, with standing flood waters exceeding a depth of 3 feet in portions of Hobe Heights and surrounding neighborhoods, where flood waters approached homes, overtopped culverts and creeks and caused dozens of roads to become fully or partially impassable. The flood waters were very slow to recede.

Training bands of heavy showers redeveloped across coastal areas of Martin County during the morning of October 2 and persisted into the early afternoon. Rain totals of 5 to 8 inches fell across the same area impacted by 6 to 10 inches only a day earlier. Many of the same areas which experienced flash flooding were again inundated with rapidly rising water, exceeding 3 feet in some areas. High water resulted in the closing of dozens of roadways. Flood waters approached many homes and intruded into several homes resulting in damage. Drainage canals and creeks overflowed and high water from the Savannas Preserve flowed into surrounding areas. The flood waters were very slow to recede.

CoCoRaHS, mesonet and Cooperative observer reports, along with reports from SKYWARN spotters and Emergency Management officials indicated that rainfall totals reached ten to over twenty inches between the early morning hours of October 1 and the early evening of October 4. Observations over twelve inches were received from seven recording stations within Hobe Sound and Stuart (highest value was from a Weather Underground mesonet site in Stuart; 20.63 inches).

CoCoRaHS, mesonet and Cooperative observer reports, along with reports from SKYWARN spotters and Emergency Management officials indicated that rainfall totals reached eight to nearly fifteen inches between the early morning hours of October 1 and the early evening of October 4. Observations over twelve inches were received from three recording stations within Jensen Beach, Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce (highest value was from a Weather Underground mesonet site in Ft. Pierce; 14.88 inches).
A 58 year old man was struck and killed by a lightning strike while grilling outdoors next to a tree.

In Saint Lucie County, sustained tropical storm force winds affected the barrier islands, with gusts to tropical storm force in squalls through much of the remainder of the county from early evening on November 8 through sunrise on November 9. The highest sustained wind was measured at the Saint Lucie Nuclear Power Plant (48 mph from the east-northeast at 1842LST on November 8) and the peak gust was also at the Saint Lucie Nuclear Power Plant (60 mph from the east-northeast at 1842LST on November 8).

Local broadcast media relayed a report of a large tree branch that fell onto an unoccupied car in Lockhart.
Lake County Emergency Management reported several trees downed by thunderstorm winds in Fruitland Park. The tree damage occurred along Sail Fish Avenue, Robin Drive, and Old Hickory Lane.

A 58-year old man from Kissimmee, Florida drowned along the Canaveral National Seashore, at Playalinda Beach. The man noticed his 11-year old grandson struggling to swim and he entered the water to assist. On their way back to shore, the man was swept under the water and disappeared for a few minutes. He then resurfaced, but was unresponsive. CPR was performed but the man died. The drowning was likely a result of a strong rip current, combined with rough surf. The grandson was injured, but survived.

Two local residents were swimming together at Juan Ponce de Leon Landing Beach in Melbourne Beach when they became trapped in a rip current. The first victim was a 23-year-old female who was unable to be revived at a local hospital. The second victim was a 26-year-old male who disappeared beneath the water. His body was recovered the following afternoon a few miles to the north of where he went missing.

A group of tourists from Indiana were visiting Cocoa Beach. A 45-year-old man attempted to aid a female member of his group who was struggling to swim after being caught in a rip current. Cocoa Beach Fire Department personnel deployed a jet ski, and the man and woman were brought to shore. The man was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The female was treated, and she survived.

A resident in Oviedo near the intersection of County Road 426 and Lee Avenue reported several damaged fences, flagpoles, a few missing shingles on a couple of homes, and damage to a couple of small trees. Photos were provided, which were consistent with localized wind gusts of 50-55 mph. A strong thunderstorm crossed the area at the time of the reported damage, which likely produced a microburst.

A resident of the Preserve Pointe subdivision on Merritt Island, just south of the NASA Causeway and west of State Road 3, observed trees being uprooted, fences destroyed and solar panels ripping off of neighbors' roofs as a severe thunderstorms passed by. The eyewitness report along with videos and photos confirmed that a brief, weak (EF-0) tornado likely developed within the thunderstorm and produced additional scattered, (mainly tree) damage northeastward to Pine Island Road. The circulation likely initially reached the ground within the Pine Island Conservation Area to the southwest of Preserve Pointe.

FAA personnel at the St. Lucie Airport observed a funnel cloud that likely formed into a waterspout over the Atlantic, approximately 2 miles offshore. Two other funnel clouds were observed in the same area.

Several weather spotters and mesonet stations recorded rainfall of 3 to over 7 inches in less than two hours. Roadways were flooded with stalled cars on S. Williamson Boulevard, south of Taylor Road in Port Orange.
The ASOS at the Treasure Coast International Airport in Ft. Pierce, KFPR, measured a peak wind gust of 34 knots from the west as a thunderstorm crossed the airfield.

A man was struck by lightning while fishing on the beach at Spessard Holland South Beach Park in Melbourne Beach. The man was taken to a local hospital with injuries. The associated isolated thunderstorm moved from the mainland across the barrier island to the Atlantic while producing occasional cloud to ground lightning strikes.

Based on information provided by the Volusia County Sheriffs Office, a short-lived tornado touched down just west of U.S. Highway 1, near the intersection of Sleepy Hollow Road, in New Smyrna Beach. Peak winds are estimated around 55-65 mph. The tornado touched down at approximately 1340LST, then traveled half of a mile east where it became a waterspout over the Intracoastal Waterway. The waterspout dissipated around 1341LST before reaching the barrier island. The tornado produced tree damage along Sleepy Hollow Road that included several medium to large-sized branches downed, and a couple of small trees knocked over. No additional damage reports were received.

The public reported downed trees and minor home damage from thunderstorm winds that occurred in Saint Cloud, near Brillante Drive in Saint Cloud. These winds are estimated at 60 mph. The damage consisted of two downed trees, awnings ripped off, backyard items tossed around, and several fences damaged.

A storm survey conducted by NWS Melbourne confirms that a severe thunderstorm produced a small area of peak straight-line winds estimated between 55 and 65 mph, mainly within the Pinecrest Subdivision of Sanford. These winds caused several large trees to snap or uproot. Numerous large branches were also downed throughout the area. A few trees and many large branches fell onto roofs and blocked roadways. Damage to a few homes, sheds, garages, and fences occurred. Surrounding this area, a larger zone of winds estimated between 45 and 55 mph impacted portions of north-central Seminole County, near and west of the Orlando-Sanford International Airport. A peak wind gust of 43 mph was recorded by the ASOS (KSFB) at 1825LST. Within this area, mostly minor damage to trees and branches was observed.

A photo posted on social media confirmed that this storm produced a brief waterspout on the St. Johns River near the State Road 50 boat ramp, just east of the town of Christmas.

A 69-year-old white male from Oregon was swimming in the surf around 1630LST off Jerry Park in Cape Canaveral (an unguarded beach) when family members lost sight of him. He was then located unresponsive in the water approximately 100 yards offshore and transported to a local hospital in critical condition where he was later pronounced deceased. Although no one saw what actually happened, his family reported feeling a strong current pulling away from shore. He was considered a strong swimmer that had visited many beaches before. Distant Hurricane Larry produced moderate, long-period swells on this day, leading to a high risk of numerous and strong rip currents. The Medical Examiner listed drowning as the cause of death.

A 58 year old male local resident was pulled from the surf unresponsive near the Daytona Beach Bandshell, which is located in the 400 Block of North Atlantic Avenue in Daytona Beach. With few witnesses around, it is unclear if the man was struggling in the water before he was spotted. He was later pronounced dead at a local hospital.

Between 4 and 6 inches of rain fell during the late afternoon hours in portions of northern Seminole County. Heavy thunderstorms that were nearly stationary produced significant rainfall accumulations in approximately 2 hours, and this resulted in localized flash flooding in the Sanford area. Standing water reached at least 2 feet in some spots, resulting in numerous road closure and several stalled vehicles. Flood waters briefly entered one home and several nearby garages. Several businesses in Downtown Sanford along 1st Street reported having 2-3 inches of water inside their establishments.

CoCoRaHS and mesonet reports indicated that between 4 and 6 inches of rain fell in just two to three hours during the late afternoon of September 19. Several observations over five inches were received from Sanford and Lake Mary (the highest value was from a Weather Underground mesonet site in Sanford; 5.90 inches). The ASOS at the Sanford International Airport (KSFB) measured 5.17 inches of rain, with 4.22 inches falling between 1600-1700 LST.

Daytona Beach Ocean Rescue and local media reported that three children (all siblings) from Keystone Heights, Florida were caught in a rip current in Daytona Beach, near the intersection of Glenview Blvd. and Highway A1A. Lifeguards pulled a 10-year-old boy from the surf unresponsive and administered life saving measures. The child was taken to a local hospital where he later died. The other two siblings were rescued and did not require medical attention.

Coastal flooding occurred along the Volusia County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. Many public beaches in the county were completely underwater during the time of high tide. Volusia County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor to moderate beach erosion, closure of a few coastal roads due to water backing up from the Halifax River, and minor damage to wooden access ramps at the beaches.

Coastal flooding occurred along the Brevard County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. At Trident Pier (TRDF1), the highest observed water level was 2.76 FT MHHW on November 7th, and a secondary peak of 2.61 FT MHHW was observed on November 8th. Brevard County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor to moderate beach erosion, and water approaching a few coastal roads due to water backing up from the Indian River. Significant water run-up occurred toward the dunes at many county beaches.

Coastal flooding occurred along the Indian River County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. Indian River County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor beach erosion. The county also reported the most impacting beach erosion occurred after the peak of the total tide heights due to the compounding effects of the successive high tides taking their toll on the beaches. Significant water run-up occurred toward the dunes at many county beaches.

Coastal flooding occurred along the Saint Lucie County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. Saint Lucie County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor beach erosion. Significant water run-up occurred toward the dunes at many county beaches.

Coastal flooding occurred along the Martin County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. Martin County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor beach erosion. The county also reported the most impacting beach erosion occurred after the peak of the total tide heights due to the compounding effects of the successive high tides taking their toll on the beaches. Significant water run-up occurred toward the dunes at many county beaches.

Extreme rainfall, with totals of 6-12 inches fell in less than 12 hours, with much of the rain occurring in less than 6-hours. Numerous roadways in Port St. Lucie, White City and adjacent Ft. Pierce South experienced rapid inundation, resulting in stalled cars and blocked roads. Numerous roads were closed with water approaching several homes. Water accumulated to heights of 2.5 to 3 feet near Kitterman Road and U.S. Highway 1 (Port St. Lucie) and Gopher Ridge Road (White City). The highest rain measurement was 11.40 inches from a Weather Underground mesonet site located 4 miles north of Port St. Lucie.
A mesonet site recorded a peak wind gust of 37 knots near the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant, along the immediate coast of Hutchinson Island as a heavy shower moved onshore.

A very slow-moving front produced persistent heavy rains across portion of Volusia County. Twenty-four hour rain totals were 6-10 inches, however most of the rain fell in less than 12-hours, impacting Daytona Beach and Port Orange. As much as 5-6 inches accumulated between 1500 and 1800 LST. Numerous roadways were flooded, with as much as 1-2 feet of standing water in some localized areas, resulting in road closures.
